summary.text: The birthday problem asks how likely it is that, among n randomly chosen people, at least two share the same birthday.
It is called a paradox because only 23 people are needed for that probability to exceed 50%.
The same maths applies to hash functions in computing, where a birthday attack reduces the work of finding a collision.

facts.label: The magic number
facts.value: 23 people give a better than even chance of a shared birthday

facts.label: Usual assumptions
facts.value: 365 equally likely birthdays, independent of other people

facts.label: Four sharing
facts.value: 187 people for a better than even chance that 4 share

facts.label: Early history
facts.value: Attributed to Harold Davenport around 1927; first published by von Mises in 1939

items.prompt: You want the chance that at least two people in a room share a birthday. Which route is the simpler calculation?

options.label: Count every pair of people and add up their matches
Find the chance that no two share, then take that from one
Find the chance for two people and multiply by the group size
List all 365 birthdays and check which ones repeat

items.explain: It is simpler to calculate the chance that no two people share a birthday, because that and a shared birthday are the only two possibilities.

items.prompt: People are added to a room one at a time. Why does the chance of having no shared birthday fall so quickly?

options.label: Each new person must avoid the birthdays of everyone already there
Each new person is more likely to be born on a busy day
Each new person adds one more day to the calendar
Each new person copies the birthday of the one before

items.explain: The second person must avoid the first person's birthday, the third must avoid both, and so on, so the chance of avoiding all of them keeps shrinking.

items.prompt: Real birthdays are not spread perfectly evenly through the year. What does that unevenness do to the chance of a shared birthday?

options.label: It lowers the chance, so the group must be larger
It raises the chance a little, but 23 people still suffice
It makes no difference at all, in theory or in practice
It raises the chance so much that 23 people are too many

items.explain: Any unevenness increases the chance of sharing, but real birthdays are not uneven enough to change much: the group size for a better than even chance is still 23.

items.prompt: An attacker wants two different inputs that give the same short fingerprint from a hash function. What does the birthday model do for them?

options.label: It makes the fingerprint impossible to ever repeat
It lets them rebuild the original input from the code
It cuts the work needed to find a matching pair of inputs
It guarantees the first two inputs tried will match

items.explain: The birthday attack uses this probability model to reduce the complexity of finding a collision, which means two inputs with the same hash.

items.prompt: Pairs sharing a birthday need 23 people for a better than even chance. For 4 people to share one birthday at those odds, would you expect about the same, somewhat more, or far more people?

options.label: Far more: 187 people
About the same: 23 people
Somewhat more: about 30 people
Fewer: about 12 people

items.explain: The source gives 187 people for a better than 50% chance that 4 share a birthday, far above the 23 needed for pairs.

items.prompt: To make the birthday problem easy to work with, which simplification do the usual models make?

options.label: Everyone is born in the same month of the year
Leap-year births are the most common of all
Twins are counted in the group more often than not
Each of 365 days is equally likely, independent of other people

items.explain: Leap years, twins and seasonal variation are disregarded, and each person's birthday is assumed equally likely to be any of 365 days, independent of the others.

paragraphs.heading: The question
paragraphs.text: The birthday problem asks a simple thing: in a group of n people chosen at random, how likely is it that at least two of them have the same birthday? The surprise, known as the birthday paradox, is that 23 people are enough to push that chance above 50%. It is a veridical paradox, meaning it looks wrong at first glance but is in fact true.

paragraphs.heading: Why 23 is enough
paragraphs.text: Twenty-three is less than a fifteenth of the days in a year, so the number feels far too small. The key is that every person is compared with every other person. Twenty-three people make (23 × 22)/2 = 253 pairs, and all 253 of those pairs get checked for a match.

paragraphs.heading: The usual assumptions
paragraphs.text: To keep things simple, leap years, twins, seasonal patterns in births and similar effects are usually set aside. Instead there are taken to be 365 possible birthdays, each equally likely, with each person's birthday independent of everyone else's. An even spread of birthdays actually gives the lowest chance of a match, and any unevenness raises it. Real birthdays are not uneven enough to matter much: real data still put the 50% mark at 23 people.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the other way
paragraphs.text: The aim is the chance that at least two people share a birthday. It is easier to find the chance that nobody does, then subtract it from 1, since exactly one of those two outcomes must occur. Line the people up. The first has no one to clash with, the second must avoid the first person's day (364/365), the third must avoid both earlier days (363/365), and so on down the line.

paragraphs.heading: Stretching the problem
paragraphs.text: With d standing for the number of days in a year, the answer stays at 23 people for any d from 341 to 372. The question can also be pushed further: how many people does it take for a better than even chance that 3, 4 or more of them share one birthday? For four people sharing a birthday, the answer is 187.

paragraphs.heading: Hashes and attacks
paragraphs.text: The same maths turns up in computing. A cryptographic attack called the birthday attack uses this model to cut the work of finding a collision for a hash function, and the model also estimates the risk that a collision already exists among a given number of hashes. The match-up is direct: the size of the hash space plays the part of the days in a year, and the number of hashed items plays the part of the people in the group. In theory, a 128-bit hash such as MD5 should keep that risk between 10⁻¹⁸ and 10⁻¹⁵, the uncorrectable error rate of a typical hard disk, until about 8.2×10¹¹ documents.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it
paragraphs.text: The problem is usually credited to Harold Davenport around 1927, though he did not publish it then. He would not call himself its discoverer, since he could not believe nobody had put it forward earlier. The first published version came from Richard von Mises in 1939.
